problem: The chapter contradicts itself on starting torque. Its own formula with s_m = 0.20 gives T/T_max = 0.38 at standstill (the table says so), and the table puts full load at 0.47 T_max. So the curve implies a starting torque of about 0.38 × 2.1 ≈ 0.8 times full-load torque — less than full load, which could not start a loaded machine. Two paragraphs later the text says a standard cage motor has 'a starting torque of roughly 1.5 to 2 times full-load torque'. A student who checks the table will find the text wrong, and vice versa.
fix: Keep the numbers consistent. Either say: 'On this simple curve the standstill torque is only about 0.4 of the pull-out torque, roughly 0.8 times full load. Real cage motors lift the starting point to 1.5 to 2 times full load by using a deep-bar or double-cage rotor, whose resistance is high at standstill and low when running.' Or drop the 1.5 to 2 figure from this section and give it only under 'Beyond', with the deep-bar reason attached.

problem: P is described as 'the number of poles per phase winding'. That is non-standard wording. A reader can easily multiply by 3 and get 500 rpm for a 4-pole motor.
fix: Write: 'P is the number of poles of the machine' (for a three-phase winding the poles per phase and the machine poles are the same number).

problem: Presented as exact, but it is the approximate form that ignores stator resistance and stator leakage reactance. Students who compare it with measured motor data will find the standstill end of the curve much too low.
fix: Add one sentence after the formula: 'This is the approximate form; it neglects stator resistance and reactance, so it is accurate near the peak and on the running part of the curve, not at standstill.'

problem: '(Chapter 3.2)' is written as plain text, so the cross-reference does not link.
fix: Use Chapter 3.2 so a reader on a phone can tap through to the induced-EMF explanation.
